idiom_name: sealed interface (unexported marker method) + struct variants + type switch with a panicking default
implementation_notes: Go has no sum types: the accepted realization is a sealed interface - an interface with an unexported marker method so that only types in the defining package can satisfy it - with one struct per legal shape carrying that shape's fields. Construction goes through constructor functions (NewConnected, ParseState) that validate their arguments, and consumption through a type switch. What replaces the sealed structure is the unexported method plus the package boundary; what is missing is exhaustiveness, because the compiler never proves that a type switch covers every variant, so keep the consumer in the defining package and give the switch a default that panics on an unknown variant, and run an external linter (exhaustive, go-sumtype, sumlint) in CI. Where states are payload-free, an integer enum plus String() and a Validate() method is the simpler Go-sized model.
pitfalls: A nil interface value satisfies the sealed interface and matches no case, so the type switch still needs its default arm to fail loudly instead of doing nothing.

Only the defining package can implement the interface - putting an implementation in another package (or an internal test package) either fails to compile or forces an exported marker method that unseals the set.

Exhaustiveness is not checked by the toolchain: without a linter in CI, adding a variant leaves every existing type switch silently incomplete, and the panic only fires on the production path that sees it.
